turn_text: Welcome back to Tell Me More, a podcast series featuring distinguished visitors to Tufts University who share their ideas, discuss their work, and shed light on important topics of the day. The week before the death of President George H.W. Bush, Tufts University's Chris Swan spoke with former New Hampshire Governor John Sununu, who served as President Bush's Chief of Staff from 1989 to 1991. Senunu reminisces about his time spent with the late President Bush while campaigning for the all-important New Hampshire primary, reflecting on the face-to-face campaign style that he says works so well in his state. He recalls how President Bush met voters over breakfast at McDonald's, Denny's, Dunkin' Donuts, sometimes as many as five restaurants in a single morning. And looking ahead, Sununu considers the crowded field of Democratic candidates for the 2020 presidential campaign and whether a Republican should challenge President Trump for the GOP nomination. Let's listen in.

turn_text: Well, look, there's always an evolution in process. I have to put it in the context of how presidents communicate. Franklin Roosevelt discovered the radio and went to his fireside chats to go directly to the people. And then John Kennedy discovered network TV, used it brilliantly. Bill Clinton discovered cable TV, tucked his saxophone under his arm and went on all those shows and talked directly to his constituency. Barack Obama was the first to make use of social media. He did it in a broad sense. And now you have Donald Trump discovering that every morning there's 50 million people who wake up to see what the dear leader has tweeted. And so this process of communication has become much more targeted to people. And yet more remote because you're not looking them in the eye. And as a result, I think it's caused much more of a sharpness to occur in the discourse. Everybody can have their own Twitter account and argue with 20,000 people that they've never even seen and be as obnoxious to them as they want and never suffer the response of a tough stare back. And if you're not looking at somebody when you're having this kind of an argument, you tend to be much more obnoxious, much more unwilling to listen to the other side at all and much more willing to come to common discourse. I've said that the problem in the country is not trying to figure out how to come together. The problem in the country is to figure out how we can continue to stand apart, but in a civil manner with civil discord. Of course, we're never going to obliterate differences. We're going to be apart in issues and desires for policy. But what we have to do is not try to figure out how to erase the differences, but how to argue for compromise in a civil way.
